Dust mites don't bite — what triggers the sneezing, itching, and morning congestion is the protein in their waste, which accumulates wherever they live. And a fabric couch is prime habitat: warm, humid from body contact, and stocked with the shed skin cells they feed on. You can't make a couch mite-free permanently, but a consistent routine keeps populations — and symptoms — low.

Three things kill or remove mites reliably: **heat above about 130°F, sustained low humidity, and physical removal with a sealed HEPA vacuum.** Everything below is one of those three in practice.

## The Routine

### 1. HEPA-vacuum the whole couch — slowly

Use a vacuum with a true HEPA filter and go slower than feels natural; quick passes lift surface debris but leave the allergen load in the weave. Do the seams, the crevices, under every cushion, and the underside. A standard vacuum without HEPA filtration can make symptoms worse by exhausting fine particles back into the air.

### 2. Wash everything removable in hot water

Covers, throws, and pillow cases go through a wash at 130°F or hotter — the temperature is what kills mites, so check your water heater setting. Dry completely on high heat.

### 3. Heat or freeze what can't be washed

Non-removable cushions can go outside on a hot, dry, sunny day — heat, UV, and dryness all work against mites. Small items like throw pillows can alternatively go in a sealed bag in the freezer for 24 hours; the cold kills mites, and a hot wash afterward removes the allergen residue.

### 4. Drop the room's humidity

Mites can't survive sustained humidity below roughly 50% — they absorb water from the air rather than drinking. A dehumidifier or consistent air conditioning in the couch's room is the closest thing to a permanent structural fix, because it makes the habitat itself hostile.

### 5. Add barriers and repeat

Washable slipcovers put a hot-washable layer between mites and you. Then the honest part: this is a routine, not a project. Vacuum weekly, wash covers every week or two, keep humidity down. Populations rebound in weeks when the routine stops.

## When the Couch Itself Is the Problem

An old couch carries years of accumulated allergen load in foam that no vacuum reaches. If you're doing everything above and symptoms persist — or the couch is 7–10+ years old, has ever been water-damaged, or [makes you itch on contact](/blog/home-cleaning/why-does-my-couch-make-me-itch/) — the load inside the cushions may simply exceed what surface maintenance can control. Our guides on [full allergen removal](/blog/home-cleaning/how-to-remove-allergens-from-couch/) and [low-allergen replacement materials](/blog/home-cleaning/best-worst-couch-materials-for-allergies/) cover the decision; when it lands on replacement, [removal is priced upfront by ZIP](/pricing/) and the old couch is out in one visit.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What kills dust mites in a couch?

Heat above ~130°F, sustained humidity below ~50%, and freezing all kill mites. HEPA vacuuming removes both mites and — just as important — the allergen residue they leave behind, which is what actually causes symptoms.

### Do dust mites bite people?

No. Dust mites don't bite; the itching and respiratory symptoms come from an allergic reaction to proteins in their waste and body fragments. If you have actual bite marks, you're dealing with a different pest.

### How often should I clean my couch for dust mites?

Weekly HEPA vacuuming and covers washed hot every one to two weeks, with humidity kept below 50% continuously. Mite populations rebound within weeks once a routine lapses.

### Can an old couch be full of dust mites even if it looks clean?

Yes — the visible surface says little about the allergen load in the foam beneath. Age, any moisture history, and persistent symptoms despite cleaning are the real indicators that the couch itself has become the reservoir.
